title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
content_html:
Three Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across three distinct timescales, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Immediate effects occur during the exercise session itself. Short-term effects appear in the hours following exercise, typically lasting up to 36 hours. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Immediate Effects: What Happens While You Exercise

As soon as exercise begins, several changes are immediately visible or measurable. The skin becomes hot, sweaty and flushed (red): core body temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, and the body responds by directing blood to the skin capillaries, where heat can radiate away. Sweating further cools the skin through evaporation. The increase in depth and frequency of breathing is driven by rising carbon dioxide levels in the blood: chemoreceptors detect this and signal the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate and tidal volume, delivering more oxygen and removing CO⊂2; more rapidly. Finally, heart rate rises to pump more oxygenated blood to the working muscles — this increase begins even before exercise with an anticipatory rise, driven by adrenaline release, and climbs further as exercise intensity increases.

Key Fact

The three immediate effects of exercise are: (1) hot, sweaty and red skin; (2) increased depth and frequency of breathing; (3) increased heart rate. These all begin during the exercise session and return to normal within minutes of stopping.

Short-Term Effects: The Hours After Exercise

In the period immediately after exercise and for up to 36 hours, the body experiences a range of short-term effects as it recovers. Tiredness and fatigue result from the depletion of glycogen (stored glucose) in the muscles and the accumulation of waste products. Light-headedness can occur as blood redistributes away from the brain toward the muscles during exercise, or when exercise stops suddenly and blood pools in the lower limbs before circulation fully adjusts. Nausea may follow high-intensity efforts, particularly in the stomach, as blood flow to the digestive system is significantly reduced during exercise. Aching, cramp and most importantly DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) develop as the micro-damage to muscle fibres — especially after eccentric contractions or unfamiliar movements — triggers an inflammatory response that peaks 24–48 hours post-exercise.

DOMS is caused by micro-tears in the muscle fibres, particularly following eccentric (lengthening) contractions — for example, lowering a weight under control, running downhill or landing from a jump. These micro-tears are repaired by the body, and during that repair process the muscle fibres are rebuilt slightly thicker and stronger than before. This is the fundamental mechanism of muscle hypertrophy. Experienced athletes experience less DOMS because their muscles have already adapted to a given level of stress. When DOMS does appear, it is typically a signal that a new training stimulus has been applied and adaptation is underway — but the soreness itself should not be severe enough to limit movement significantly.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations in multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it.

Body shape may change: regular resistance training increases muscle size and reduces relative body fat, while prolonged endurance training may produce a leaner physique with visible muscular definition. Specific components of fitness improve: muscular endurance, speed, suppleness, muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance and stamina all increase with appropriately designed training programmes. For example, a sprinter who trains over many months will improve their speed and explosive strength; a cross-country runner will develop greater cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance in their legs.

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are cardiac hypertrophy and bradycardia. Cardiac hypertrophy refers to the heart growing larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump more blood per beat — a greater stroke volume. Because stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output. This produces bradycardia: a lowered resting heart rate. While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 beats per minute, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm. Mo Farah, for example, is reported to have had a resting heart rate in the low 40s during the peak of his marathon career.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → cardiac hypertrophy (the heart grows larger) → greater stroke volume per beat → bradycardia (lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output). These are all long-term adaptations — they take months or years of consistent training to develop.

Hypertrophy as a general term refers to the growth in size of a muscle caused by an increase in the size of individual muscle fibres. When applied to skeletal muscles (e.g. the biceps or quadriceps group), it is the result of progressive resistance training: repeated eccentric and concentric contractions under load cause micro-tears, which repair larger and stronger over time. When the term is used specifically as “cardiac hypertrophy,” it refers to the same growth process applied to the heart muscle itself, driven by the sustained cardiovascular demands of endurance training. In both cases, the underlying stimulus is the same — the body adapts to repeated stress by growing the muscle tissue — but the practical outcomes differ: skeletal muscle hypertrophy increases strength and power for movement, while cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume and reduces resting heart rate.
